en: An Explanatory Preface to the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things" Ordinary people perceive movement within that which does not transmigrate; the wise perceive non-transmigration within movement. Therefore it is said:
what people call "movement" is because things of the past do not reach the present; what I call "stillness" is likewise because things of the past...

It has not reached the present, yet some have criticized it, claiming that Master Zhao’s assertion that "what existed in the past is non-existent now" constitutes a doctrine of annihilationism, eternalism, transmigration, or cessation.
This is most certainly not the case. I have once composed a verse on this matter: "In the past, it was simply the past; The past did not come from the past to become the present."

The past exists only in the present; the present does not go to the past. The present neither goes nor comes. By this, one knows that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are eternally abiding.
Some, however, cling to the medicine and thereby contract the disease, or mark the boat while searching for a lost sword; their lack of wisdom is extreme.

This is the origin from which Master Ji’s "Explanation on the Non-transmigration of Phenomena" emerged. When the sun illuminates the four worlds, there is originally no sequence, yet the spatial directions remain profound and fixed.
Nevertheless, the wise person uses the sun-dial to observe it, whereas the fool handles the sun-dial in reverse, and his orientation of the directions is likewise inverted.
To clarify this for the public, I have engraved the method for handling the sun-dial and circulated it.

Preface to the *Discourse on the Non-Transmigration of Things* and its Exegesis, composed by the Layman Zhenshi, Bing Mengzhen, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the Jichou year of the Wanli era:

The ultimate void is without things; things are not things, for they all transcend the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*). Non-transmigration is transmigration, yet it is neither transmigration nor non-transmigration. Together—

"Extinction. Indeed, the forms of things are devoid of substantiality; transformation depends on non-transformation, which is what the mind and intention penetrate, and what can be reached through verbal expression.
How could this not be the profound purport that movement and stillness are not different? Nevertheless, as for what is called "the non-transmigration of things":

It is not that there is no thing, nor that there is no non-thing; it is not that there is movement, nor that there is no movement. Rather, one merely relies on the Dharma to eliminate attachments, as illness must be treated with medicine.
Thus, for those who cling to the notion of permanence, non-transience is taught to clarify transience; for those who cling to the notion of transience, transience is taught to clarify non-transience.
These are all provisional names used to guide beings and excellent medicines prescribed according to their ailments. How then could the principle of non-transience—?
Is it possible to conceive of "transmigration" or "non-transmigration"? Yet some, by relying on medicine, instead fall ill; they feel for what is empty and mistake it for reality.

Failing to understand the statement that "all things abide according to their own nature," they suppress and refute the principle that the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
This is one dream. My subsequent attempt to debate this is yet another dream. Thus, it is neither transmigration nor non-transmigration.
How could the principle of non-transmigration possibly be communicated through such dream-like talk?
Nevertheless, to awaken from a dream by means of that very dream, it is likewise impossible to do so without discourse. Let those of like mind resolve this.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Zhènjiè of Shuāngjìng, on the first day of the first month of autumn in the Dīngyǒu year of the Wànlì era.

A critical commentary on the "Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things" by the Śramaṇa Zhènjiè of Zhuīlǐ. A Critical Commentary on the "Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things" By the Śramaṇa Zhènjiè of Zhuīlǐ. [The text follows with the commentary itself.]

Now, the passing away and renewal of birth and death, and the alternating succession of cold and heat—these are the constant conditions of the flux of things, which is the common experience of ordinary people.
This describes the delusions of such ordinary people and serves as the introduction to the *Treatise on Non-Transformation*.

For ordinary people claim that birth and death, coming and going, mutually succeed one another in transformation; and that cold and heat, coming and going, alternate and shift. Yet they do not realize...
All phenomena are from the beginning eternally quiescent. Originally, there is no body or mind, nor birth and death; likewise, there is no cold or heat, nor coming or going.
For this reason, through deluded perception one sees things as shifting, yet fails to realize that things do not shift.

That which is called "the non-shifting of things" refers to the fact that while the phenomenal forms of things may be observed and thus designated as "things," the essence of these things is quiescent, and for this reason they are termed "non-shifting. This is non-shifting.
Therefore, each and every thing is inherently quiescent within its own place. Because things exist as objects, they mutually depend upon one another in relation to the four images (*catur-nimitta*).
Yet, the nature of things is without differentiation; when realized, it is the True Principle (*tattva*). The Truth is fundamentally unchanging, and things are themselves serene and still.
It is due to the limitations of ordinary perception that one falsely perceives motion within the unmoving—what is called "the clouds moving, the moon traveling, and the boat moving."
The shore shifts. Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "If one realizes that the true mind is unmoving, then the myriad dharmas do not undergo change.
If one perceives the shifting and passing away of the myriad dharmas, these are all the deluded mind; for all objective realms are merely the deluded movement of the mind.
If one is separated from mind and consciousness, there is not even a single dharma that is permanent, let alone the migration of myriad dharmas. Therefore, [the text] explains this extensively below.
This is done by citing scriptural and treatise-based statements to refute [the opponent].
I, however, maintain that this is not the case. Why? The *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Phenomena have no coming or going; they do not move or shift."

This reverses the preceding [arguments] to clarify non-transmigration. Now, the essence of all dharmas is devoid of the characteristics of coming and going, and lacks the characteristic of movement and change.
Why is this? It is because all dharmas arrive through the convergence of conditions; yet in their arrival, they come from nowhere.
They depart when conditions disperse; yet in their departure, they go nowhere. Thus, within coming and going there is no coming and going, and within movement and change—
There is no movement or transition. Therefore, the *Ratnāvalī* states: "Dharmas have neither coming nor going; they are without movement or transition.

Nevertheless, ordinary people do not realize that what arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature and thus has no coming or going; consequently, they falsely perceive the coming and going of all phenomena.
Thus, regarding the body, they see birth and death alternating; regarding the world, they see cold and heat shifting in turn. Out of compassion for them, the Master [Nāgārjuna] then...
This Dharma establishes its thesis by being without coming or going and without movement or transition, in order to refute the view that permanent persons and flowing entities undergo motion.
Now, consider this "action of non-movement": it does not seek stillness by abandoning movement; rather, one must necessarily seek stillness within all movements. One must necessarily seek...

Quiescence is stillness amidst all movement; therefore, although there is movement, it is always still. One does not abandon movement in order to seek stillness; therefore, although there is stillness, it is not separate from movement.
This is the fundamental intent behind the formulation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings, serving as the basis for composing this treatise. Indeed, it is the state of non-movement—
This work does not consist of abandoning movement to seek stillness; rather, it necessarily seeks stillness within movement. Thus, movement and stillness are not different.

Therefore, in the following text, it is said that "change is itself non-change" to clarify that change is not different from non-change, and it is said that "non-change is itself change" to clarify that non-change is not different from change.
Thus, movement and stillness have never been different from the outset, yet those who are deluded perceive them as distinct.

Consequently, true words are obstructed by contentious debate, and the path of the fundamental principle is stymied by a love for novelty. Therefore, the ultimate nature of stillness and agitation is not easily discussed.
This is presented to clarify the difficulty of establishing a definitive statement. However, since movement and stillness are not different, then change and non-change are likewise not distinct.
Because they are not different, one may move and yet not move; thus, it cannot be called merely "moving. One may not move and yet move;
thus, it also cannot be called merely "not moving. Yet, those who are deluded differ in their views regarding this movement and non-change.
Change and non-change are not the same. Because they are not the same, those who cling to change call it "change," while those who cling to non-change likewise call it "non-change.
This causes the truth beyond words to become mired in contentious debate, and the doctrine of non-differentiation to be eclipsed by a fondness for difference.
Thus, the fact that movement and stillness are not different is not easily explained.

Why is this? For to speak of the Truth is to oppose the world; to conform to the world is to deviate from the Truth. Because one deviates from the Truth, one is deluded regarding one's nature and cannot return to it;

because one opposes the world, one’s words are bland and tasteless. This causes those of middling capacity not to distinguish between existence and non-existence, while those of inferior capacity clap their hands in derision and pay no heed.
That which is near yet unknowable—what else could it be but the nature of things? Yet they are unable to realize it themselves.
[The preceding section] has concluded. For now, I shall briefly direct my mind to the juncture between movement and stillness. How could this be said to be absolute?
To investigate and explain the reasons why it is difficult to speak [of this], he immediately concludes by citing the nature that is difficult to know in order to initiate his discourse.

Why is it so difficult to speak of the extremes of stillness and agitation? This refers to the explanation provided below in the "Discourse on the True. It means that if one speaks of non-transmigration, it will contradict...
To follow change is to oppose non-change; to oppose non-change is to lose sight of one's nature and fail to return to it.

To go against change is to speak of things as bland and flavorless, such that those of middling capacity hear it and feel as if it exists yet does not exist, while those of inferior capacity hear it and clap their hands in derision without a second thought.
Now, I wish to discuss non-change without opposing change, and to explain change without contradicting non-change, so that—

That those of middling and inferior capacities, upon hearing this, each attain faith and understanding is truly not easy to express; hence, the ultimate distinction between stillness and agitation is likewise not easily described.

Therefore, while ordinary people say that past things do not arrive in the present, and the Master of the Treatise also says that past things do not arrive in the present—even as they speak of non-transmigration, they do not depart from transmigration; thus, they do not contradict transmigration.
Because it speaks of non-transmigration by means of non-opposing transmigration, the meaning is profound and flavorful;

thus, it enables those of middling and inferior capacities who hear it to each attain faith and understanding. Furthermore, the passage below states that "human life passes swiftly, swifter than a flowing stream.

This likely describes transmigration in contrast to those who calculate [existence] as permanent, speaking of movement and cessation through the lens of non-movement and non-extinction. Although the words seem to imply transmigration, [it is not so].

Movement is itself non-movement; thus, it does not contradict non-movement. Because movement is spoken of without contradicting non-movement, one who is deluded regarding their nature can return to it.
Therefore, when those of the Two Vehicles hear this, they attain awakening and realization, for the realization of the Way is itself the truth.
Thus, the ultimate state of non-differentiation is not only difficult to express in words, but also extremely difficult to know.
Therefore it is said: "That which is near yet unknowable—is it not simply the nature of things? Although it is difficult to speak of and difficult to know, one cannot help but proceed.
Thus, I have briefly entrusted my mind to the juncture of movement and stillness in order to clarify transition and non-transition.
How could this be called definitive? It is because in explaining transition, one does so precisely by means of non-transition to clarify transition; how could it be otherwise?
Regarding "change," the teaching of non-change is precisely the use of change to clarify non-change; how could it necessarily be non-change?
Therefore, it is said that movement and stillness are merely provisional designations, not something absolute.
Let us attempt to discuss this: Daoyuan says, "All dharmas fundamentally come from nowhere; in departing, they likewise go nowhere.
The *Mādhyamaka-śāstra* states, "By observing the directions one knows that there is going, yet the goer does not arrive at any direction. These all seek stillness within motion;
thus it is clear that the non-transmigration of things is made manifest through such knowledge.
This citation of scriptural and treatise-based statements serves to clarify non-transmigration (*akṣaya*).

Generally speaking, all phenomena (*dharmas*) have a source from which they come and a destination to which they go; this may be called transmigration. However, since they come from nowhere and go nowhere, and phenomena do not arrive at one another, they are therefore non-transmigratory.
To say that one knows the departure of the "other" by observing the direction is like a person traveling from the east to [the west].
Regarding the west: when viewed from the perspective of direction, it appears as if there is going; thus it is said, "Observing the direction, one knows that there is going.

As for "going does not reach a direction," this means that going has no place to which it goes. Therefore, a verse in the *Śāstra* says: "There is no going in what has already gone, Nor is there going in what has not yet gone.
Apart from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, There is also no going in the 'present going'. The *Commentary* states: "It is like a person who is initially at..."

Standing upright and unmoving in the east is called "not yet having gone. Because it has not yet gone, that which has not yet gone cannot be called "going," for the phenomenon of going has not yet arisen.
If one takes a single step away from one's original standing place and looks back toward that place:
Then it is called "already gone. Because it is already gone, that which is already gone cannot be called "going," for the process of going has already ceased.
To delude people, one might then argue: "Going exists where there is motion; herein lies the time of going, which is neither 'already gone' nor 'not yet gone.
Therefore, going occurs during the time of going. Nāgārjuna then refutes this by means of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*), saying: "If there were an 'already gone'..."
If there were no "already gone" and "not yet gone," there would be no "time of going.
It is like how there is length in the middle because of shortness at both ends; if there were no shortness at both ends, there would be no length in the middle. Therefore, the verse says:
"Apart from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, there is no going in the time of going either. This demonstrates that there is no going in the three times.
Going has no place to which one goes; it is not that "no-going" constitutes going. Therefore it is said: "The goer does not arrive at a destination.

These [points] below synthesize the intent of the sūtras and śāstras, whose fundamental tenet is non-transmigration (*apravṛtti*). However, this principle of non-transmigration is profound and subtle, difficult to clarify.
Now, I shall further manifest it through concrete phenomena. For example, when a person goes from the first step to the third step, if the first...
When the first step goes away, the second step comes; when the second step goes away, the third step comes.

Thus there is going and coming, which is what is meant by "movement. However, whatever involves going and coming belongs to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Since it belongs to dependent origination, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since it lacks intrinsic nature, its entire substance is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If this is so, then [this is] the foremost.

One steps away; yet in departing, there is no place to which one departs. One steps back; yet in arriving, there is no place from which one comes. It is thus with one step; it is thus with every step.
From this, one knows that all dharmas are such that within departure and arrival there is neither departure nor arrival, and within movement and turning there is neither movement nor turning.
Therefore it is said: "Seek stillness within movement to know that things do not shift; seek non-shifting within shifting..."
There is no transmigration; how could there be any entity that can be moved?
What people call "movement" is based on the fact that past things do not arrive in the present; therefore, they say it is movement rather than stillness.
What I call "stillness" is likewise based on the fact that past things do not arrive in the present; therefore, I say it is stillness rather than movement. As for movement...
It is not still because it does not come; it is still yet not moving because it does not go.
This is precisely using the transition of ordinary people to clarify non-transition.

For ordinary people say that things of the past do not reach the present, seeing that the things of the past have transitioned away from the past and thus do not arrive at the present. Therefore, it is said: "moving yet not [truly] moving."
"Quiescence. This refers to not realizing that what arises through conditions has no inherent nature; thus, one perceives things as shifting and passing away, which is why it is called "movement.
The Master [Sengzhao] maintains that past things do not arrive in the present because he perceives that past things arise through conditions and lack inherent nature.

Since they have departed, they do not depart [as substantial entities]; therefore, they do not reach the present. Thus, he says it is quiescent rather than moving. This is the thorough realization of dependent origination.
Because there is no inherent nature, departing is itself non-departure; this is why it is called stillness.
Movement is not stillness because that which does not come has already shifted away in the past, and thus does not come.
Stillness is not movement because that which does not depart has already departed in the past and thus does not depart.
That being so, since all things of the past have already followed conditions into emptiness, they neither go nor come. What thing is there that can be moved?
Thus, the view of transmigration fades away, and the principle that the nature of all dharmas is empty becomes clear.
Yet, some individuals fail to comprehend Master Zhao’s insight into the principle that dependently arisen phenomena lack intrinsic nature, and further misinterpret "quiescence."
Rather than being moved, it does so by virtue of its non-departure;

thus, he [Sengzhao] concluded that what the Master said regarding "past things not arriving in the present" was like the previous boat carrying fish and the subsequent boat carrying bamboo shoots—the fish from the previous boat remain in that very boat.
Since the former vessel does not reach the later one, you therefore use the fact that the former object remains in the past and does not come to refute it;
this is merely the erroneous interpretation of some person. How could it be the vision of Master Zhao?

Furthermore, as for "quiescent and not moving because it does not go," this is because the conditions of the former object have separated and departed; since departing is itself non-departing, it is called "not going."
It does not mean that a thing of the past remains in the past and does not depart.

Yet, some individuals, having mistakenly interpreted the passage concerning "remaining still and not departing," proceeded to refute [the doctrine] by claiming that things of the past remain in the past and do not go. Thus, one knows that their interpretation is untenable both in terms of its literary style and its underlying principle.
Furthermore, these individuals fundamentally failed to comprehend the principle of the non-transmigration of things elucidated by Master Sengzhao. Moreover...
Regarding the *Qingliang Shuchao*, it is said that Master Zhao’s statement that "things do not shift" (*wu buqian*) is confused with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Consequently, [the critic] relies upon those words to suppress and refute him. This, however, fails to understand the intent of the *Shuchao*.
For the *Shuchao* states that Master Zhao’s statement that "things do not shift" is confused with the Lesser Vehicle because it is based on the treatises of the Lesser Vehicle.
It says: "Conditioned phenomena arise at this very place and perish at this very place; there is no possibility for them to transfer from here to another location. The *Chao* commentary explains:
"Arising here and perishing here without reaching another location is identical in meaning to the principle of non-transmigration (*bujian*).

Yet, there is a dharma-substance that arises and perishes; therefore, this is not the Mahāyāna. The Mahāyāna teaching holds that what arises through conditions is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Arising...
That which arises does not arise; that which ceases does not cease. Therefore, "change" and "non-change" are diametrically opposed in principle.
However, Master Zhao’s treatise contains two meanings. What is clarified in the manifest text mostly accords with the former meaning.

This is likely because Master Zhao’s intention was to regard the fact that each phenomenon abides in its own nature as "non-change," thereby conflating it with the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) view that there is no possibility of moving from this [state] to another.

This is because [the two truths] are distinct. However, the subsequent treatise states: "In discussing the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is the designation of 'non-transmigration'; in guiding the mundane world, there is the discourse on 'flux.
This takes the ultimate truth as non-transmigration, yet it does not reveal the characteristics of the ultimate truth.

If one merely employs the principle that each thing abides in its own nature as the characteristic of the ultimate truth, how could this not be the emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā), wherein nothing can transmigrate? End of citation.
All of these are excerpts from the commentaries (*śāstra*). However, since the commentaries state that they contain two meanings, they do not pertain solely to the Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "what is clarified in the manifest text mostly accords with the former meaning," this is because the principle that "things each abide in their own nature" shares many textual and semantic similarities with the Hīnayāna doctrine that there is no possibility for things to move from this place to another location; yet in actual principle, they are vastly different. Moreover...

It is said: "If it were merely that each thing abides in its own nature that constitutes the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), would this not be the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), wherein nothing can be transmuted?
For ultimate truth is the sublation of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-nirvāṇa*).

Since you take the abiding of each thing in its own nature as the characteristic of ultimate truth, is this not precisely taking the absence of things and the absence of abiding as the ultimate truth of non-transmigration? Therefore:
Yongming also stated: "What Master Sengzhao called 'the abiding of nature' (xingzhu) takes the absence of nature as its very nature.
Since he regards the emptiness of nature—the True Truth—as non-transmigration, how could it be conflated with the principle of arising and ceasing found in the Lesser Vehicle?
Even if Qingliang claimed this was conflated with the Lesser Vehicle, he did not say it was identical to the views of ordinary worldlings. As for the aforementioned person who, based on past...
If one objects that "things abide in the past and do not come," then one is suppressing [the truth] and aligning oneself with the common views of ordinary people.
If this were so, one would not even be equal to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), let alone be able to dwell securely in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) while conflating it with the Small Vehicle.
Thus, this not only fails to accord with the textual meaning of the commentaries, but also contradicts the intent of the words upon which it relies.

This is contradictory and truly lamentable. Furthermore, some individuals, failing to comprehend Master Sengzhao’s clarification that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature and thus free from coming and going—this state of stillness—erroneously claim that Master Sengzhao asserts that "past things remain in the past and do not go" as being stillness.
If there were things and their abiding, this would constitute the conditioned; and if it is conditioned, it is subject to arising and ceasing. How, then, could this be [stillness]?
To call this "quiescence" is merely the erroneous interpretation of certain individuals; how much less could it be the vision of Master Sengzhao!
This is precisely what is meant by seeking fault within that which is faultless. It is not only a slander of the Dharma, but also a deception of others.
Furthermore, to claim that one is not refuting Master Sengzhao, but rather refuting "what the world considers right," is likewise [incoherent].
This not only deceives Master Zhao alone, but also treats all people under heaven with contempt.

I reflect privately that the reason this person incurs the crime of slandering the Dharma and deceiving others is not due to any other intent, but simply because he fails to understand the principles of the texts. How can one not be careful?
Thus, that which is created has never been different, yet that which is perceived has never been the same. What is called "obstruction" is simply following the contrary;
what is called "passage" is simply following the natural flow. If one truly attains the Way, what further impediment could there be?
The "Manifestation" (Ming) and the "Superior Creation" (Shangzao), though identical in substance, differ in their perspectives. Indeed, things of the past do not reach the present; they are but one.

Nevertheless, what is perceived truly differs according to whether one is deluded or awakened. Thus it is said: "What is created has never been different, yet what is perceived has never been the same.
Because perceiving the shifting and passing away of things runs counter to the unarisen and eternal, and because this [delusion] obstructs [the truth], it is called "running counter" (ni).
What is called "obstruction" is when one sees an object and cannot let it go; thus, one conforms to the truth of non-arising. Because one uses this to achieve penetration, it is called "conforming.
If one truly awakens to the fact that every object arises through conditions and lacks intrinsic nature—thereby being non-arising—one will not be detained by coming, going, moving, or shifting.
Therefore, it is said: "If one attains the Way, what more could possibly obstruct?"
It is a pity that human sentiments have been deluded for so long. One faces reality with one’s own eyes yet fails to perceive it;
knowing that past things do not return, one nevertheless claims that present things can depart. Since past things do not return, where could present things go? Why is this so?
If one seeks the object of the past within the past, it was never absent there; yet if one demands the object of the past within the present, it has never existed here.
That it has never existed in the present clarifies that the object does not come; that it was never absent in the past makes it known that the object does not go.
One conceals the past while seeking the present; yet the present, too, does not go forth.
[The author] laments how ordinary people are deluded, and exhaustively explains that dharmas have no going or coming, thereby clarifying that things do not transmigrate.

Those who face reality with their own eyes yet remain unaware are told that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*): unmoving and unchanging, they never depart from their proper place and are eternally present.
It is inherently tranquil, yet ordinary people do not perceive it in their daily lives; this is why the sages lament it.
Having understood the passage below, it reiterates the point above to clarify that things of the present and the past do not reach one another.

That is to say, if one knows that past things do not come into the present, then how could present things go back to the past? The section following "past things" reiterates and confirms this [non-arrival].

Regarding the meaning of "mutual non-arrival": Why is this? Below, the text investigates and debates the principle that things do not arrive at one another in order to establish the doctrine of non-transmigration, thereby refuting the view that flowing entities possess movement.

When it says, "Seeking the object of the 'present' within the 'present,' it has never been non-existent," this means that the object of the present arises through conditions and lacks intrinsic nature;
thus, though it departs, it does not depart, and though it is non-existent, it is not non-existent. Therefore, it is said that within the present, it has never been [non-existent].
"Non-existent" does not mean that the object previously facing [the observer] remains facing it while becoming non-existent.

Furthermore, because ordinary people see the object move away and cling to the notion that it is gone, this clarifies that movement is itself non-movement, and non-existence is itself not non-existence.
This is precisely using the movement perceived by ordinary people to clarify non-movement. If one seeks the object from its current state, it has never existed there.
This means that since the preceding entity, having arisen through conditions, lacks intrinsic nature, it does not persist into the present; therefore, what existed previously does not exist now.

In the section "In the present," the author restates and clarifies that the preceding entity does not come. In the section "In the future," the author restates and clarifies that the preceding entity does not go.
Thus, the reason why the preceding object does not "go" is that the preceding object departs because its conditions have ceased;
once it has departed, it no longer exists, and is therefore said not to go. This does not mean that the preceding object remains stationary in its prior state and does not depart.
Yet some people fail to understand the meaning of this explanation, and instead fall into the error of regarding the former existence as eternalism and the present non-existence as nihilism.
I refute this. Is it not like criticizing a swift horse for its galloping while blaming a lame donkey for its inability to walk fast?

To seek further and claim that the present does not go because the past did not come is to say that since the past object lacked intrinsic nature due to its dependence on conditions and thus did not come, the present object likewise lacks intrinsic nature due to its dependence on conditions and thus does not go. Indeed, the non-going of the present object is also...
"Going is itself non-going. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "For example, like the waters in a river, rushing and competing in their swift flow, each unaware of the others;

so it is with all phenomena. This means that while the rushing current flows on, it does not obstruct the fact that each wave arises from conditions, lacks intrinsic substance, and yet does not reach the others. Therefore, they are mutually unaware of one another. It is just as it is right now.

In the past, although things vied with one another to go forth, they do not obstruct one another; for all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature, and thus there is no mutual coming and going.
Therefore, each does not reach the other. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All phenomena have no substantial nature, nor do they possess any functional activity;
therefore, they are all entirely unaware of one another. Now, since this [teaching] holds that every phenomenon arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature...
By observing their coming and going, one clarifies that there is no transmigration; this is precisely using transmigration itself to clarify non-transmigration.
Furthermore, how could the deluded discourses of "existence previously and non-existence now," or of "annihilation, permanence, transmigration, and extinction," be permitted to interfere with this?
This means that past things exist in their own past; they do not come from the present to reach the past. Present things exist in their own present;
they do not come from the past to reach the present.
This demonstrates that past and present things each do not reach one another. The first two phrases demonstrate that the present does not reach [the past].

In the past. The final two lines demonstrate that what existed in the past does not reach the present. As for the statement, "The so-called 'objects of the past exist in the past,'" it means that objects of the past do not come [to the present] but appear as if they remain in the past;
therefore, it is said, "Objects of the past exist in their own place in the past.

They do not migrate from the present to the past, and thus they do not proceed from the present to the past. Objects of the present do not depart [for the future] but appear as if they remain in the present; therefore, it is said, "Objects of the present..."
"It exists in the present; it does not migrate from the past to arrive at the present. Therefore, it does not proceed from the past to the present.
Thus, the present and the past do not reach one another, and phenomena do not arrive at one another. What substance is there that could possibly migrate?

Consequently, what is called 'the thing of the past existing in the past' and 'the thing of the present existing in the present' is truly because things of the present and the past lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) due to their dependence on conditions."
There is no coming or going; it is conventionally designated as "being," yet in reality there is no location where it exists. For "being" is equivalent to "coming and going";

since there is neither coming nor going, how could there be "being"? Therefore, Qingliang [Xuanzang] took the fact that each phenomenon abides in its own nature to be the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus one knows that every thing is no-thing, and even its "being" is non-being. This means there is neither going nor coming, nor is there any place of abiding;

therefore it is called "non-transience. Yet some people stubbornly cling to the literal words without grasping the underlying meaning, and consequently refute [the doctrine] on the grounds that things exist and have a location. Do they not thereby invite for themselves the error of being wrongly censured?
Therefore, Zhongni said: "Hui, you see the new; those who cross arms are not the same as those of old.
He cites this to prove that things of the present and the past do not reach one another.

When he says one sees the new rather than the old, it means that the new and the old arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, and thus do not reach each other: the new does not reach the old, and the old does not reach the new. Thus it is.
To see the new as not being the old: although this new and old are drawn forth from conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they do not transition into one another.
To use this as proof that things of the present and the past do not transition into each other precisely demonstrates that all phenomena arise from conditions and lack self-essence;
therefore, they do not mutually cognize or reach one another.
Thus, it is clear that things do not come and go from one another. Since there is not even the slightest trace (*liṅga*) of coming or going, what thing could possibly be moved?

This concludes the previous point that past things do not come to the present and present things do not go to the past. Regarding the statement "there is not even the slightest trace of staying or returning":
This means that present things, being devoid of intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, do not depart from the past; therefore, they do not go.

Likewise, things of the past, being devoid of intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, do not arrive at the present; therefore, they do not return. Since there is not even the slightest trace of coming or going, what entity could possibly be moved?
Thus, even as whirlwinds topple mountains, they remain eternally still; though rivers rush together in torrents, they do not flow; though wild horses gallop and race, they do not move;
and though the sun and moon traverse the heavens, they do not complete their circuits. What cause for wonder is there?
This illustrates the principle of being unmoved while moving, thereby establishing the logic of being non-transmigrating while transmigrating.
To express this in terms of inference (*anumāna*): the subject (*dharmin*) is "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); the predicate (*sādhya-dharma*) is "transmigrating yet non-transmigrating."

The reason is stated as follows: "Because each and every thing arises through conditions, lacks intrinsic nature, and does not mutually reach one another. The parallel example states: "The preceding wave is not the subsequent wave," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "each and every thing arises through conditions, lacks intrinsic nature, and does not mutually reach one another," it is because each thing is empty due to its dependence on conditions;
thus, they do not come and go. For instance, waves arise from conditions and lack substantiality, and therefore [do not reach one another].
They appear to arrive. Therefore, all phenomena shift yet do not shift. Thus, the *Zongjing* commentary explains: "The preceding wind is not the succeeding wind;
therefore, though it topples mountains, it remains eternally still. The preceding wave is not the succeeding wave; therefore, though they rush together, there is no flowing."
The preceding breath is not the succeeding breath; thus it wafts and stirs without remaining still. The preceding day is not the succeeding day;

thus it traverses the heavens without completing a cycle. Since this is the fundamental principle of reality, what is there to be wondered at? In this way, the three members [of the syllogism] are free from fault, and the thesis (*pratijñā*) is successfully established.
Yet some people ultimately claim that Master Sengzhao’s formulation of the doctrine of the ultimate is flawed because the reason (*hetu*) is non-existent and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is absent.
As for the cause: it is because they have misunderstood Master Zhao’s intention. Why is this?

Master Zhao originally clarified the principle of non-transmigration by means of the fact that things have no coming or going; he did not clarify non-transmigration by means of the existence of things or their abiding.
Yet, certain people having misinterpreted his meaning, they consequently took the existence of things and their abiding as the cause of non-transmigration; hence it is said, "There exists..."
The Master has no cause for this, yet he indulges in reckless talk regarding Prajñā and erroneously reviles the former sages; how can this not be debated?
Now, this debate is not merely to refute the person of Mr. He; it is also intended to clarify what that person has failed to understand.
For while Mr. He himself may be set aside as a single individual, those who have been deluded by his words cannot necessarily be dismissed with such ease.

It is difficult to bring this to an end. How could I, indeed, delight in disputation? It is only because I fear that those who misunderstand my words might likewise fall into the pit of slandering the Dharma.
Alas! A Sage has said: "The life of man passes away as swiftly as the flow of a river. For this reason, the Śrāvakas realized what is not [the ultimate truth].

One constantly attains the Way through these conditions. For the Pratyekabuddha, awakening to conditions means departing from them to realize the ultimate reality. If the myriad movements were not transformations, how could one seek the Way by following those transformations?
Re-examining the words of the Sage, they are subtle, hidden, and difficult to fathom; they appear to move yet remain still, and seem to depart yet stay behind.
This can be apprehended through the spirit, but it is difficult to seek through phenomena.

This passage cites the words of the Sage to clarify "non-transmigration. Someone may ask: "The previous discussion spoke of non-transmigration; why then do you now speak of transmigration? The answer is:

The previous statement said "non-transmigration" because it was addressed to those who cling to the notion of transmigration; it was precisely by means of transmigration that non-transmigration was clarified.
"Change is not different from non-change. This is said in response to those who calculate [existence] as eternal; therefore, it is again called "change.

This means that by means of non-change, one clarifies that change is not different from non-change. Thus, for the followers of the Two Vehicles, awakening to cessation is precisely non-cessation, and change is precisely non-change, thereby establishing that the Way is identical to the Real.
"Gǒu wàn xià" (If, below, ten thousand... explains what has been realized. "Gǒu" means sincerity. "Fēi huà" (not transformation) means not...

"Change" (*qiān*) means "to seek" (*xún*), which is "immediacy" (*jí*). This is because that by which the two vehicles accomplish the Way and realize the Truth is precisely that all phenomena are in constant motion yet do not change.
Thus, one awakens to this as the basis for attaining the Way; it is not by means of immediate change that one attains the Way. Re-examine what follows below.
This clarifies that the words of the Sage are difficult to fathom. If one says "movement" and so forth, it clarifies the reason why they are difficult to fathom.

This is because the Sage speaks of movement and transition precisely while there is neither movement nor cessation. Therefore, though there is movement, in reality there is no movement; though it appears to transition, in reality there is no transition.
Thus, if one meets this through the spirit, one realizes that there is neither movement nor cessation, thereby attaining accord with the non-transient. If...
If one seeks it through phenomena, one sees only its movement; therefore, it is said that it can be realized through spiritual resonance (*śen-hui*) but is difficult to seek through phenomena.
This concludes the clarification of movement and non-movement.
Thus, it is said that "departing is not necessarily departing," to dispel people's habitual conceptions; and "abiding is not necessarily abiding," to release people's [attachments].
This refers to what is called "going. How could it be said that because something goes, it can be sent away, or because it stays, it can be retained?
This presents the meaning of the two preceding sections.

As for the statement, "Going is not necessarily going," etc., it is because by explaining change as being identical to non-change, one speaks of change without it differing from non-change; therefore, there is no necessity for change. It is merely to prevent [misunderstanding].
This is merely the common conception of people. To speak of "non-transmigration" is to employ transmigration itself to designate non-transmigration;

it is not different from transmigration, and thus it need not be a non-transmigration. It simply explains the destination of people's [conceptions]. Thus we know that in speaking of transmigration and non-transmigration, one only seeks to dispel the emotional attachments of people;
fundamentally, there is no fixed doctrine to be expressed. How could one take transmigration as transmigration? Or...
That which does not migrate is indeed non-migratory. Therefore it is said: "How could one say that what has departed can be sent away, or that what remains can be retained?
Thus, the *Chengju* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) states: "The Bodhisattva dwells amidst those who cling to permanence, yet expounds the teaching of impermanence; this is the Mahāyāna."

The Treatise says: "All dharmas are immovable; they have no place from which they come or to which they go. These words all guide and reach toward the various quarters; two statements converge upon one truth.
How could it be said that Mañjuśrī deviates from this ultimate principle?
This serves to cite evidence for the meaning of the two preceding sections. First, a scripture is cited to prove transience;
second, a treatise is cited to prove non-transience. "The various directions" refers to the manifold methods employed to guide beings according to their needs.

The statement that "the two are one in principle" means that explaining transience is not different from explaining non-transience, and explaining non-transience is not different from explaining transience. Although this is so—
While the words are spoken differently according to the capacity of the listener, the essential principle of transition and non-transition is no different. Thus it is said:
"How could one say that Mañjuśrī deviates from this principle?

Therefore, though it is said that the eternal does not abide, and though it is called departing, there is no transition. Because there is no transition, although there is movement, it is eternally still.
Because it does not abide, though it is still, it is constantly moving; because it is constantly moving while still, it moves without shifting;
because it is constantly still while moving, it is still without lingering.
This summarizes the meaning of the two preceding sections. For it was previously stated that non-transmigration is not different from transmigration;
thus it says, "to speak of permanence yet not to abide. Not abiding is precisely transmigration. The subsequent passage states that transmigration is not different from non-transmigration.
Therefore it is said that although one speaks of "going," there is no transition. Because there is no transition, although there is going, there is no transition.

Because there is no abiding, although there is no transition, there is going. Although there is no transition yet there is going, therefore one goes without transitioning. Although there is going yet there is no transition.
Therefore, it does not move, yet it moves. In this way, moving and not moving have never for a moment been different;
it is neither moving nor not moving, yet we merely name it "the non-moving of things.

Previously, when I elucidated the non-moving of things through the principle that all dharmas are empty by nature, that was the non-moving of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is what is meant by "non-moving yet moving."

To say that there is movement yet no movement, or that it is neither moving nor non-moving while clarifying that things do not move—this is the non-movement of the Middle Way’s primary truth (paramārtha-satya).
How could others possibly conceive of this through the dualities of movement and non-movement?
Thus, Zhuangzi’s reason for hiding his mountains and Confucius’s reason for gazing upon the river were both prompted by the realization that the past is difficult to retain;
how could they have intended to reject the present in order to go toward it? Therefore, one who observes the mind of the Sage does not perceive it in the same way as ordinary people do.
This answers the objection raised by outsiders to clarify the meaning of how the Sage’s responses to external stimuli differ. Some may say:
"The previous discussion stated that movement and non-movement are not different. Yet, when Zhuangzi hid his mountain and Confucius faced the river, were these not instances of movement?
The answer is: That which led Zhuangzi to hide his mountain and that which led Confucius to face the river—these are all...

It is for those who fail to perceive the constant flux that one feels the difficulty of retaining what has already passed; how could this be the same as the worldly view that excludes the past and clings to the present?
Therefore, it is said that those who contemplate the mind of a sage do not attain their realization through the same perceptions as ordinary people.

Why is this? People assume that youth and vigor constitute the same entity and that a hundred years are but a single substance; they merely perceive the passage of time, yet fail to realize that the physical form follows along with it.
For this reason, when a Brahmin who had left the household life returned with white hair, his neighbors saw him and asked, "Is that still the same man from before?
The Brahmin replied, "I am the same person as before, yet I am not the person of before. All the neighbors were astonished, for his words did not accord with their expectations.

It is as the saying goes: "The strong carry it on their backs and run, while the ignorant remain unaware. Is this not what is meant? This serves as evidence to explain the meaning of the passage regarding the departure of the deceased.
Why is it that for a sage, once he has departed, it is difficult to retain him? [The text notes: "As for humans, they are inferior.

This cites an actual event to explain the meaning of the passage regarding the departure of the deceased; it implies that people of the time knew only that a hundred-year lifespan is but a single physical form.
Unaware that every thought-moment undergoes transformation and decay, a Brahmin returned with his hair turned white. When a neighbor saw him, he remarked, "The man from before still lives.
Seeing that the Brahmin had not yet awakened to this truth, the neighbor immediately alerted him with these words: "I am still the same person as before."
That they are not people of former times—is this not precisely the intent of Zhuangzi and Confucius? Yet the neighbors still do not realize that the physical form has undergone transformation;
thus, they all stare in astonishment and condemn his words. This is no different from what Zhuangzi meant by:
"At midnight, a strong man carries one away and runs, yet the deluded do not perceive it"—the neighbors' failure to realize the transformation of the form is exactly like this.
Thus it is said: "Is this not what is meant?
For this reason, the Tathāgata, responding to the points where the various dispositions of sentient beings were obstructed, employed local dialects to resolve their delusions.

Relying upon the non-dual true mind, he emitted diverse and manifold teachings. That which remains consistent despite these apparent divergences—surely that is nothing other than the words of the Sage. Therefore...

In discussing ultimate truth, there is the designation of "non-transmigration"; in guiding the mundane world, there is the teaching of "flux. Although these thousand paths may sing different melodies, they ultimately converge upon the same destination.

This concludes by clarifying that while the Tathāgata’s teachings differ according to the capacities of his audience, they do not contradict the single consistency [of the ultimate truth], thereby fulfilling the preceding statement.
The ultimate aim is one and the same. "Dialect" (*fāngyán*) refers to words spoken in response to specific capacities; it is the remedy for treating afflictions. Hence, it is called "dialect.

This is because the obstructions of sentient beings' minds are not uniform; therefore, the Tathāgata, relying on the single true mind, prescribes remedies according to their ailments and preaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities.
Although there are a thousand differences, the underlying principle does not vary. Thus, it is said that they may appear divergent, yet they are not [ultimately] so.

Is there anything more distinct than the words of the Sage? Therefore, following the discussion of the True [Dharma], this concludes that although the expressions differ, their ultimate meaning is one.
Now, those who examine the text hear of "non-transmigration" and claim that past things do not arrive in the present;
hearing of "flux," they claim that present things can reach the past. Since we speak of "past" and "present," why would one wish for them to transmigrate? For this reason, he speaks of "going."

There is no need to go; it has existed constantly throughout antiquity and the present because it is immovable. To say one "goes" yet does not go means that one does not proceed from the present to the past.
Because it does not come, it does not race through the past and the present; because it is immovable, each nature abides within its own single age.
Thus, although the texts of the various canons differ and the doctrines of the hundred schools vary, if one attains their essential convergence, how could they be different?
How delusive are literary expressions!
This is said in response to those who are hindered by texts and stuck on words; it clarifies that one who thoroughly understands principle is not deluded by literary phrasing.
Indeed, all dharmas taught are merely in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings. How could there be any fixed dharma to be taught? Furthermore, how could it be...
How could one allow for grasping through literal adherence? Yet those who seek the meaning in the text fail to realize this intent and thus grasp it literally.
Consequently, upon hearing that "there is no shifting," they claim that past things do not reach the present; hearing of "constant flux," they further claim that present things can reach the past.
Therefore, for those who again cling to the notion of shifting, I clarify non-shifting precisely by means of shifting.

This dispels the view of grasping at things according to their literal names. Since it is said "below," one hears those who argue that because things flow and change, present objects can reach the past;
therefore, he first uses the principle of non-transmigration to establish the ground.

Thus, in the section "below," he correctly clarifies the meaning of transmigration and non-transmigration, thereby dispelling the view that takes transmigration as actual transmigration. This refers to what is called: "when speaking of going, it is not necessarily going," and so forth.

It is because when the Sage addresses those who calculate permanence, although he speaks of the succession of past and present and the transformation of phenomena, this does not preclude the fact that all things of the past and present arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
Since change is itself non-change, he speaks of change to demonstrate that things do not change; thus it is said:
"When one speaks of 'going,' it need not mean going; when one calls it 'departing,' it need not mean departing. This is because when one speaks of going...
Because the past and present do not pass into one another, the ancient remains fixed in the ancient, and the present remains fixed in the present;
thus it is said that the ancient and the present exist eternally. This is because each abides in its own state without movement.

Since what is called "the past" does not depart from the present, the present does not go to the ancient; therefore, there is no transition from the present to the ancient. This is because the ancient [remains as it is].
Because the present and the past exist [simultaneously]. Now, since the present and the ancient do not come and go between one another, one does not gallop through the present and the ancient;
and since the present and the ancient both constantly abide without movement, each nature dwells within its own single age.

Yet, since this is spoken of as "abiding" by means of the non-transmigration of that which arises through conditions across the present and the ancient—being devoid of inherent nature—one knows that this abiding of nature is [precisely] because...
"Non-existence is its nature; non-abiding is its abiding. Therefore, Yongming said that what Master Zhao (Sengzhao) referred to as "nature and abiding" means that "non-existence is its nature.
If this is so, then even the nature of the past and present cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any abiding?
Furthermore, Qingliang also took the fact that "each thing abides in its own nature" to be the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). How could he have [meant] that things exist?

Is there such a thing as a "dwelling" that constitutes the characteristic of ultimate truth? Yet some individuals, failing to comprehend the meaning of ultimate truth as being without intrinsic nature and without dwelling, instead refute it by asserting the existence of intrinsic nature and dwelling. Is this not to speak falsely of Prajñā?

Furthermore, since the present and the past do not come and go between one another, one knows that to say something has "gone" is not to say it has gone; to say it has "departed" is not to say it has departed.
To depart and listen to that which flows—how could one take "going" as going, or take "departing" as departing, and yet claim that a present thing can reach the past?
Thus, the view that the present migrates to the past is refuted. Therefore, it follows that those who penetrate the underlying principle below are not deluded by literary expressions.
The diverse texts of the various scriptures refer to the words of the many sutras; the hundred schools differ [in their phrasing].
Regarding the discourse on the assembly of teachings: it clarifies that those who have realized the underlying principle understand that both transition and non-transition are taught.

Furthermore, the various texts and differing explanations serve merely to dispel the emotional attachments of sentient beings; fundamentally, there is no fixed dharma, nor is there any ultimate divergence in meaning.
Therefore, one should not be deluded by the phrasing of the words, nor should one grasp at them as being literally true.
Therefore, what others call "staying," I call "departing"; what others call "departing," I call "staying.
Thus, although departing and staying differ, their ultimate purpose is one. Hence the Sūtra says: "Right words seem contrary;
who would believe them? These words have their basis in this very principle.
This section clarifies the meaning of the distinct expressions having a single significance, demonstrating that one should not grasp at them according to the literal words.
For what others call "abiding," I speak of as "going. Yet, although I speak of "going," it does not contradict "abiding.
This is because "going" is spoken of in terms of being without movement and without cessation; therefore, it does not contradict abiding. Furthermore, regarding what others call "going," I...
It is said that it "abides. Yet, although it is said to abide, this does not contradict its movement.

Because one speaks of abiding on the basis of the fact that coming and going are themselves without coming and going, it does not contradict movement. Thus, while the words for "movement" and "abiding" differ, their ultimate significance is no different.

How could one possibly grasp at things according to their literal expression? Therefore, the scripture says [the following], citing evidence to show that although the words differ, their ultimate meaning is one.

As for "the literal statement being correct while the apparent meaning seems contrary," this means that when it is said that "going" departs from reality, it does not contradict "abiding"; and when it is said that "abiding" dwells in reality, it does not differ from "going."

Therefore, it is said that they appear contradictory. As for the question, "Who would believe this?"—because the meaning of how these divergent words lead to a single realization is likely beyond the reach of speech and thought, it is difficult for people to believe. It is not only difficult to believe, but also difficult to fathom;
as previously stated, "it can be realized through the spirit but is difficult to seek through phenomena. Thus, there must be a reason for what the scripture says regarding belief.
Why is this? People seek the past within the present and claim that it does not abide; I, however, seek the present within the past and know that it does not depart.
If the present were to reach the past, the past would have to contain the present; if the past were to reach the present, the present would have to contain the past.
Since the present contains no past, one knows that it does not come; since the past contains no present, one knows that it does not go. If the past does not reach the present, then the present...
Nor does it reach the past; each phenomenon abides in its own nature within a single world-period. What thing, then, could come or go?
This is a refutation of the meaning of the [opponent's] words, further providing a detailed analysis of non-transmigration.
Why is it that while others speak of "going," I speak of "abiding"? This is the lower explanation. It is because ordinary people believe that the past can migrate to the present; therefore—

To seek the past within the present and claim that the past does not abide—this is what people call "transmigration. I, however, speak from a lower standpoint to clarify what I mean by "non-transmigration.
To say that one seeks the present within the past and knows it does not depart means that because the conditions of the present arise without intrinsic nature, they do not depart from the past;
thus, while seeking the present within the past, [one finds it] within the past.

"There is no present. Therefore, we know that the present does not go to the past. "If the present were to reach the past" (Section 1) reverses the argument to demonstrate the principle that the present and the past do not reach one another.
"The present, however, does not exist in the past" (Section 2) follows the argument to clarify the principle that the present and the past do not reach one another.

"If the past does not come to the present" (Section 3) restates and concludes the non-transmigration to refute the notion of transmigration; thus, the view that the past migrates to the present is refuted.

However, all the preceding and subsequent passages clarify non-transmigration by means of transmigration; this is intended so that people may realize non-transmigration through the very fact of transmigration.
Thus, there is a profound reason why the title of the treatise is "The Non-transmigration of Things."

Thus, the four images (the seasons) gallop like the wind, and the celestial sphere (the *xuánjī*) rolls like lightning; yet, when one grasps the meaning down to the finest detail, though it is swift, it does not turn.
This citation uses the phenomenon of "change yet no change" to establish the preceding discussion on how the ancient and modern are both changing and unchanging.
The "four images" refers to the four seasons; when all four seasons are complete, another year has passed. The "celestial sphere" refers to the seven stars of the Big Dipper (*Beidǒu*).
A single day and night constitutes one full cycle of the heavens; this is because it signifies transition.

As for the statement regarding attaining the meaning of even the most minute [phenomena], it means that if one truly realizes that what arises through conditions has no inherent nature and thus lacks even the slightest intentionality of coming or going, then although the four seasons may rush like the wind and the celestial sphere may whirl like lightning, they cannot cause one to undergo transmigration.
Therefore, the merit of the Tathāgata flows through ten thousand generations and remains eternally present; his Way penetrates across a hundred kalpas and becomes ever more firm.
A mountain is formed by relying on the accumulation of the first basket of earth; a long journey is reached by depending upon the first step. This is because achievements and merit cannot decay.
Because achievements and merit cannot decay, although they belong to the past, they do not transform; because they do not transform, they do not shift; because they do not shift—
Therefore, it is profoundly serene and luminous. Thus the Sutra says: "While the three calamities pervade all things, one's karmic actions remain profoundly serene.
One may truly believe these words.
This presentation above demonstrates that while the past and present do not shift, the Tathāgata’s path and practice likewise do not shift. The Path is...
The principle realized is such that karma is the very cause of what is cultivated. Because the cause is true, the fruit is not erroneous;

thus it endures through ten thousand generations and remains ever-present, becoming increasingly firm throughout a hundred kalpas. From "forming a mountain" downward, metaphors are cited to clarify that meritorious deeds do not perish.
From "the fruit" downward, the conclusion is drawn through the Dharma. Indeed, the formation of a mountain begins with the first basket of earth.
It proceeds by beginning with the first basketful of earth. Yet, at the very start of that first basketful, one cannot say it is either extinguished or not extinguished.
Why? If the first basketful were extinguished, upon what could the mountain depend to be formed? If the first basketful were not extinguished, the initial soil would still persist;
how then could the form of the mountain manifest? Since it is so with the first basketful, it is likewise with the first step. From this, one may know.
That which is called "the past cause being neither transforming nor shifting" actually means it transforms yet does not transform, and shifts yet does not shift;
therefore, it is said to be "neither transforming nor shifting. This does not mean that the past cause remains fixed in the past as something unchanging and thus non-shifting.
Yet, some people, failing to comprehend the meaning of "transforming yet not transforming" and "shifting yet not shifting," falsely take the past cause— [...to be the ultimate reality].
Those who dwell in antiquity yet fail to transform [their views], while criticizing Master Zhao, must surely be misrepresenting the former sage.

Therefore, the scripture states below, citing evidence that meritorious deeds do not perish. Whereas the preceding section discussed non-transiency in terms of objects and time, this clarifies that the meritorious deeds of the Tathāgata are non-transient;
thus, one knows that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are all non-transient.
Why is this? The effect does not coexist with the cause; rather, it is through the cause that the cause gives rise to the effect.

Since the cause does not perish in the past, and the effect does not coexist with the cause, and since the cause does not come into the present—neither perishing nor arriving—the principle of non-transmigration becomes clear.
Furthermore, why be deluded by going and staying, or hesitate between movement and stillness?
This inquiry and explanation clarify why past causes neither transform nor perish, thereby concluding the principle of non-transmigration. Why do past causes neither transform nor perish?
Because the fruit does not descend. This is the explanation. It is because cause and effect follow conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
Each is individually quiescent and does not reach the other; thus, the fruit does not reach the cause, and the cause does not come to the fruit.
Therefore, they do not coexist. Nevertheless, although they do not coexist, it is not precluded that the cause produces the fruit through successive causes.

That the cause which produces the fruit does not perish in the past means that it perishes yet does not perish. That the fruit does not coexist with the cause and the cause does not come to the present means that it does not perish.
And yet it ceases. Since it does not cease while ceasing, and ceases while not ceasing, it cannot be called "ceasing," nor can it be called "not ceasing.
Thus, it is neither ceasing nor not ceasing, neither migrating nor not migrating; yet it is named "non-migration.
Therefore, the ultimate principle of non-migration is clearly revealed. How could one still be deluded or hesitant regarding migration?

It is indeed a state beyond transition. However, this section is explained by the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) through the application of the meaning of the "Eight Negations" from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
For those who wish to understand it in full detail, please consult that text.
Thus, it is not because the heavens and earth are overturned that one says they are not still; nor is it because the great floods reach the heavens that one says they are moving.
If one can harmonize with the spirit through the very objects before them, then this can be known without going far.
This passage addresses the matter of movement within stillness. To claim that wisdom merges with principle and the object meets with the spirit is something to be realized through silent awareness;
it cannot be known through words, thought, or conceptual discrimination. Thus, the *Zongjing* commentary states:

"If one can touch the object to clarify the fundamental principle and accord with the spirit through things themselves, then even if heaven were overturned and earth turned upside down, and the oceans were to boil..."
When a mountain collapses, one does not yet perceive even the slightest sign of movement; how much less so the illusory transformations and echoes that follow?
Therefore it is said: "If one can harmonize the spirit with the immediate reality of things, then [the truth] is not far and can be known.
All who investigate the mind should reflect deeply on this; do not allow yourself to obscure your own numinous spirit, nor speak recklessly of *prajñā* while falsely disparaging the former sages.
By doing so, one incurs the sin of slandering the Dharma; it harms not only oneself but others as well. Be cautious!
Be cautious!
*The Discourse on the Non-Transmigration of Things: A Critical Exposition* concludes.
I have been bedridden in a mountain ravine, reclining beneath a north-facing window.

When Master Huanju Jie arrived from Shuangjing, he brought me a copy of his commentary on the "Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things" (*Buwqian lun*) and showed it to me, requesting that I provide words as a preface. Thereupon, I wrapped myself in my robes and rose, ordering a youth to read it aloud so that I might listen.
Its main thesis centers on the quiescence of all phenomena (*dharmas*), while further evaluating them through the three [criteria].
Zhi Rong, by means of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), did not merely adhere to the words of the Master, but rather brought forth the meaning beyond those words.
His intent was profound and his expression was clear and manifest. As for me, I have always been dull-witted and ignorant;
now, being both ill and old, my brush and inkstone have gathered dust, such that I cannot even manage my immediate affairs. How could I possibly sustain this for even a single breath?

Past and present, the divine essence is realized within the flux of change yet remains unmoving; this is the profound purport. [The author] declined the request with all his might, but could not prevail.
Thus, he has written these rambling words as a postscript on the final leaf.
On the day of the Universal Gate Manifestation in the *dingyou* year of the Wanli era, the śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Old Hangzhou respectfully appends this colophon.
I have heard that only those who enter the state of non-arising (anutpāda) truly know the kṣaṇa. Thus, in the *Pañcāśad-upamā-sūtra*, a bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My transgressions are extinguished; why do I not perceive the sign of their extinction? The Buddha asked: "Can your minds undergo transformation and rebirth? He replied:
"If my mind were not to undergo transformation and rebirth, I would be unable to be in communion with the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said, "When your minds undergo transformation and arise, do you perceive the initial appearance of the mind as it first arises? They replied, "We do not know.
The Buddha said, "Since you do not know the initial appearance of the mind's arising, how could you alone know the appearance of the cessation of offenses?
By observing this very point, one sees that whether the mind transforms or does not transform, both the appearance of arising and the appearance of ceasing do not transcend this single [reality]."
It is but a mere *kṣaṇa*. Yet, as for things being non-things, shifting or not shifting—how could they possibly transcend this?
By this I know that those who refute the discourse on non-transience and argue for it do not understand the *kṣaṇa*; for them, the realization of non-arising remains far off.
To refute and refute, to debate and debate—is this not like striking at the moon with a staff? Thus, even I cannot avoid being called a man of many words.
Jiù. Postscript by Ming Shi Daguan.
